notes.meaning: Anyone who wanted to give thanks to the LORD could bring a grain offering of fine wheat flour. The worshiper poured olive oil over it and placed frankincense on top. This bloodless gift was a way to praise God for providing daily food. Bringing the finest sifted flour showed that God deserves our very best.

The person brought the mixture to Aaron's sons, the priests, who scooped up a handful of the flour and oil along with all of the frankincense. The priest burned this portion on the altar as a memorial, which was a sign asking God to remember the worshiper with favor. The burning incense made a sweet smell that was pleasing to the Lord. This burning handful represented the dedication of the entire gift to God.

All the flour left over after burning the handful belonged to the priests for food. God used this offering to provide daily meals for Aaron and his family while they served at His altar. It was called most holy, which meant only the priests were permitted to eat it within the sanctuary courtyard.

God also allowed the grain offering to be baked at home before being brought to the sanctuary. It could be baked in a clay oven as thick cakes kneaded with oil, or as thin wafers brushed with oil. Both kinds had to be made without leaven, or yeast, so that the offering remained pure.

A worshiper could also cook the fine flour and oil on a flat iron griddle over the fire. After baking, the person crumbled the bread into small pieces and poured more oil over it. Breaking the bread prepared it so the priest could easily take God's portion for the altar and keep the rest.

Another option was to cook the fine flour and oil in a deeper pan, frying or boiling the dough. God accepted offerings made in ordinary kitchen pots so that even poorer families could bring an acceptable gift. The Lord cares about a willing and humble heart rather than expensive tools.

After the bread was cooked in any of these ways, the worshiper brought it to the priest at the tabernacle. The priest then carried the gift to the altar on the person's behalf. This reminded the people that they could not approach God on their own, but needed an appointed mediator to present their gifts.

The priest took out a memorial portion from the baked bread and burned it on the altar fire. This burning part acted as a sign of thankfulness, showing that the whole offering belonged to God. The Lord accepted the rising smoke as a pleasing aroma because it came from a devoted heart.

The rest of the cooked bread belonged to Aaron and his sons to eat. God made sure that the priests who spent their lives ministering at the altar were fed from the people's gifts. Because this food was most holy, the priests had to treat it with special honor and reverence.

God strictly commanded that no yeast or honey could ever be burned on His altar. Leaven puffs up dough and causes decay, making it a picture of pride, hypocrisy, and sin. Honey also ferments easily when heated and stood for worldly pleasures that turn people away from pure devotion to God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition notes that leaven and honey were excluded to teach believers to put away deceit, carnal pleasures, and pagan worship customs.

notes.meaning: Offerings of firstfruits, which were the very first crops gathered at harvest time, could include yeast and honey. These firstfruits were brought to the Lord to thank Him for the harvest, but they were never burned on the altar fire. Instead, God assigned them directly to the priests for their own food.

Every grain offering and every animal sacrifice had to be seasoned with salt. In Bible times, salt kept food from spoiling and served as a sign of lasting friendship and covenant loyalty. Adding salt showed that God's covenant with His people was permanent, pure, and unbreakable.

An Israelite could also present an early grain offering straight from the fresh, first-ripe ears of the harvest. Because these green ears were soft and moist, they were roasted over a fire and then rubbed to separate the grain. This voluntary gift allowed farmers to thank God right away for the promise of a full crop.

The worshiper poured olive oil and frankincense over the roasted grain, just like the regular flour offering. The priest then burned a memorial handful of the grain and oil on the altar, along with all of the frankincense. The sweet incense pointed to the prayers and intercession of Christ, which make our service acceptable to God.
